0ar5g0.title: Inefficient access
0ar5g0.body:
Resolved: same fieldIndex lookup as #5nhvz2 -- a single O(1) access to
the field's handles instead of scanning meta.fields for a name match.

1k51l3.title: Library Anti pattern. Use common.SystemError
1k51l3.body:
Resolved: common.SystemError satisfies error as well as
providing means to add richer error context, which is
invaluable in tracing issues from low level utilities such
as this one, if and when such errors impact higher level
implementations.

1kkx9p.title: Migrate to document package
1kkx9p.body:
.
DocumentSet represents a collection of documents with batch operations.

2ya2hp.title: Cache Poisoning
2ya2hp.body:
`ModelCollection.FindByID` serves a document
 that was written inside a transaction that later rolled back

397ju0.title: Refactor out helpers #cruft
397ju0.body:
Resolved by removal: typeHash32/fieldHash32/fieldKeyOf and the
structFieldKey hash-bucket scheme were deleted outright when the map was
re-keyed on the natively comparable (reflect.Type, string) pair. There are
no hash helpers left to extract, and the collision-verification caveat they
existed to mitigate is gone by construction.

5nhvz2.title: Inefficient field access
5nhvz2.body:
Resolved: FieldTag now does a single fieldIndex.Get(type, fieldName)
lookup (composite-keyed, see field_tag_map.go) followed by a linear scan
of that field's handles for the tag key. Both are O(1)/O(k) with k = tags
per field (single digits) instead of the original linear scan over every
field followed by a linear scan over that field's tags.

a23h8y.title: Inefficient access
a23h8y.body:
Resolved: structMetadata now carries byKey, a map[string][]tagRef built
once in buildMetadata alongside the rest of a type's metadata. KeyTags
reads meta.byKey[tagKey] directly, so its cost is proportional to the
number of matching tags, not to the total number of tags on the type.

ah4hqh.title: Put doesn't recurse into TypeUnknown / TypeArrayUnknown
ah4hqh.body:
Put recurses into TypeArrayObject before clearing, and the doc explains
that TypeRecord holds no pool children. But TypeUnknown is any and
TypeArrayUnknown is []any — either can hold a *DataContainer. The spec
says union values live in TypeUnknown, and arrays of union elements in
TypeArrayUnknown. If a union variant is ever a nested Document, Put leaks
it.

Same root cause in copyField: TypeUnknown and TypeArrayUnknown copy the
value directly (dst.SetUnknown(key, v)), sharing any *DataContainer
pointer with the source. Releasing both would double-free.

We have two options:
(a) Enforce the invariant that these slots never contain pool-managed
children. Document it on SetUnknown, SetArrayUnknown, and Put, and add a
debug-build assertion. This matches the codebase's style (freePosition
already panics on invariant violation) and is cheap..
(b) Handle it by recursing in Put and deep-copying in copyField. More
robust if the invariant might be violated, but adds a type switch on a
hot path.
Given the spec's union language ("can hold a scalar, array, map, or open value"), (a) is probably right — but it should be explicit, not implicit.

cd05t4.title: Unneccessary computations
cd05t4.body:
Resolved: ValueKind is now computed once per tag in buildMetadata and
packed into 2 previously-unused bits of the handle (bits 60-61). Tag.
ValueKind() is now a bit-mask extraction with no string scan. See
computeValueKind and the handle layout documented on the Tag struct.

cwzt7j.title: Relocate Schema Extraction Logic
cwzt7j.body:
The schema extraction logic in this file (e.g., SchemaFrom, ExtractDTOSchemaDirect, etc.)
is a generic facility for deriving schemas from struct types using struct tags.
It does not belong in the `data` package, as it is not specific to data-layer concerns.
It should be moved to a dedicated package
once the ongoing schema pipeline optimizations are complete.
Until then, it remains here to avoid breaking dependent code during active development.

dcd001.title: Dense decoder doesn't mirror the encoder's docView fast path
dcd001.body:
inverted.go's encoder is SBE-class on the populate path: viewDoc captures
the document in one Walk (one positions lookup per field), caches slot
pointers per used DataType, and reads values via (*(*[]T)(v.slots[dt]))[idx]
with zero map access on the hot path. scanPacketBodyAs + putPacketBody
then walk res.byType[dt] — a pre-computed per-DataType field list — so the
outer loop is a fixed 16-iter type walk and the inner switch is jump-table
predictable.

dense.go's decodeDenseBody was not built to the same standard. Per field it
calls doc.SetBool / doc.SetNull / readFieldPayload, and SetXxx does, in order:
  1. type check (key.Type() != TypeX) — redundant, decode already dispatched
  2. positions[int64(key)] lookup
  3. claimHole(TypeX) — backward scan of d.holes
  4. write at [idx] (or AppendXxx if no hole)
  5. positions[int64(key)] = idx
So per field decode pays ~2 map ops + 1 hole scan + 1 append, where encode
pays 1 map op (amortized into viewDoc) + 1 array read.

This is the umbrella for #dcd002-#dcd006. The fix pattern already exists in
inverted.go: decoder should use doc.Walk to capture slot pointers and
per-field indices once, pre-size each used type slice from the state map
count (mirroring how the encoder sizes from state map counts), and write
directly through slot+idx — one positions write per field, no hole claim,
no type check, no growth.

Expected: decode-wide64 drops from ~2-4x the encoder's latency to ~1.5-2x,
and pooled decode hits 0 allocs/op.

Resolved: decodeDenseBody was rebuilt to the encoder's standard — one
state-map validation pass counts exact per-type values, PreSize sizes each
used slot once (no append growth), scalar types read and append inline with
the dispatch hoisted per type, and all writes go through the AppendXxx
decode primitive (no positions probe, no hole claim). Dense wide64 fresh
decode dropped 9.403us -> 8.312us (-11.6%); reuse 3.541us -> 3.333us; pooled
allocations on the scalar tiny shape fell 3 -> 1 per decode (the remaining
one is the pre-existing top-level byteReader escape). The full
"decode ~= 1.5-2x encode" goal is bounded by inherent array-value
allocations (21 array-typed fields each materialize their slice); pooled
scalar decode is at 1 alloc, not 0.

@see #dcd002
@see #dcd003
@see #dcd004

dcd002.title: decodeDenseStateMap allocates []fieldState; Columnar already shows the fix
dcd002.body:
Confirmed by columnar.go inspection: decodeColumnarBlock does NOT allocate
a []fieldState. It reads the packed field-major state column in place via
stateAtBit(packed, bit), a single array-index + shift + mask. Dense should
do the same for its state map — the encoder's putPacketBody writes it with
the same bit-shift pattern, so the decoder can read it with the same.

This is now a local comparison: two decoders in the same package, one reads
the state bits in place (Columnar) and one materializes a slice (Dense).
Following Columnar's lead here removes the allocation with no new design.

Same applies to any future state-map-like decoder (e.g. Stream packets if
they land): read the bits, don't materialize the slice.

Resolved: decodeDenseStateMap is gone. decodeDenseBody reads the packed
state map in place via columnar.go's stateAtBit — the []fieldState
materialization is removed, and the same single pass validates the reserved
0b11 code and counts per-type values for pre-sizing.

@see #dcd001

dcd003.title: Decoder doesn't pre-size typed slices; AppendXxx grows from cap 8
dcd003.body:
DataContainer.initSlice defaults to cap 8. For a fresh (unpooled) container
decoding 64 values of the same type, AppendXxx grows 8 -> 16 -> 32 -> 64 ->
128: ~5 reallocations plus copies per type. This dominates the "fresh"
variant of BenchmarkDecodeDense/wide64.

The encoder sizes its output exactly by scanning the state map first
(inverted.go:scanPacketBodyAs). The decoder has the same information: after
reading the state map it knows exact counts per DataType (nInt, nFloat,
nString, ...), so it can pre-size each used slot with slot(dt, nDt) before
the value loop. One allocation per used type, zero reallocations.

Resolved: after the state-map pass the decoder knows exact per-DataType
counts and calls DataContainer.PreSize(dt, n) for each used type — one
allocation per used type, zero append growth. wide64/fresh allocations fell
54 -> 46 per decode (the remainder are the 21 array fields' value slices,
which are the decoded values themselves), and BatchRows/fresh B/op fell
79.2KB -> 60.8KB per 100-record batch.

@see #dcd001

dcd004.title: SetXxx does redundant type check + unnecessary hole scan on decode path
dcd004.body:
data_container.go: every SetInt/SetFloat/SetString/... starts with
    if key.Type() != TypeX { return ErrTypeMismatch }
and then calls claimHole(TypeX), a backward scan of d.holes for a matching
type. On the decode path both are wasted work:

  - The type comes from wf.fd.DataType(); the decoder dispatched on it a few
    instructions earlier. The check cannot fail on valid input, and on
    invalid input the decode already produced garbage.

  - doc was either freshly allocated (holes empty) or Clear()'d by the pool
    (Clear resets holes to [:0]). claimHole scans, finds nothing, returns -1,
    and AppendXxx runs. Decode pays for a scan that cannot succeed.

The direct-write path from #dcd001 skips both: the write is typed by
construction and a fresh decode never reuses freed slots. If the decoder
can't adopt Walk for some reason, a fallback is a Container API variant
"SetFromEmpty" that skips type check + hole claim for known-typed fills.

Resolved: readFieldPayload became fillValue and every decoder now writes
through the typed AppendXxx API. The positions-map probe and hole-claim
scan (guaranteed no-ops on a fresh/Clear()ed/pool-fresh decode target) are
gone from the decode path; AppendXxx's own type check remains as one
well-predicted branch that also keeps the identifierMask guard. Sparse
additionally validates its wire field count against the schema so a
hostile count cannot drive unbounded appends.

@see #dcd001

dcd005.title: Sparse and Batch inherit every Dense issue; confirmed across all decoders
dcd005.body:
Inspected sparse.go, batch.go, columnar.go. Status per issue:

  #dcd001 (Walk fast path)  — ALL FOUR decoders miss it. Dense, Sparse,
                               Batch-Row (via dispatch), Columnar all use
                               doc.SetXxx per field.
  #dcd002 ([]fieldState)    — Dense only. Columnar reads bits in place.
                               Sparse has no state map. Batch inherits
                               whichever decoder it dispatches to.
  #dcd003 (no pre-size)     — All four. Sparse too: many present fields
                               still grows via AppendXxx.
  #dcd004 (redundant checks)— All four. Every SetXxx pays type check +
                               hole scan on a fresh/pooled container.
  #dcd006 (readFieldPayload)— All four call it. Single lever, four wins.

Fix pattern: one shared "fillFromReader" helper that walks the target
container once, pre-sizes from field count (sparse) or state-map counts
(dense / batch-row / batch-columnar), and writes through slot+idx.
One helper, four decoders.

Resolved: the shared helper is fillValue (dispatch.go) — Dense, Sparse,
Batch-Row (via the dense/sparse paths) and Columnar all write through it,
with no SetXxx left on any decode path. Dense additionally hoists the
scalar dispatch per type and pre-sizes from the state map; Sparse and
Columnar keep field-major loops (wire order there is per-field, so the
per-field dispatch stands). Measured: BatchRows/decode/pooled -14.6%,
BatchColumnar/decode/pooled -6.3%, nested20 decode -9% to -19% across all
container lifecycles, no regressions elsewhere.

@see #dcd001
@see #dcd006

dcd006.title: Verify readFieldPayload isn't re-dispatching per field
dcd006.body:
decodeDenseBody iterates res.byType[dt] — the same pre-computed per-DataType
grouping the encoder uses — which is correct. But then it calls
readFieldPayload per field. If readFieldPayload switches on wf.fd.DataType()
again, the grouping's benefit is thrown away: dispatch is paid once per field
instead of once per type.

Confirm by reading readFieldPayload's body. If it does switch, inline the
per-type read into the outer type loop so the dispatch cost is paid once per
type (mirroring inverted.go:putValue's structure, where the switch is on
wf.fd.DataType() but the caller has already grouped by type).

Resolved: readFieldPayload did switch per field; it is now fillValue.
Dense routes its scalar types (int/float/string, plus the bool block)
through inline per-type loops, so the dispatch is paid once per type;
complex types and the Sparse/Columnar field-major loops call fillValue per
field, where the block-constant type keeps the branch predictable.

@see #dcd001

dcd007.title: readBoolBits allocates []bool per bool block; caller iterates and discards
dcd007.body:
dense.go:decodeDenseBody and columnar.go:decodeColumnarBlock both call
readBoolBits, which returns a fresh []bool per bool block. The caller then
iterates the slice and calls doc.SetBool on each element, then discards the
slice. Two costs compound:

  1. The []bool allocation itself (one per Dense bool block; one per bool
     FIELD per Columnar block — Columnar pays it N times where Dense pays
     it once).
  2. The intermediate slice prevents direct writes into the target
     container's bool slice via Walk.

The encoder's mirror (putPacketBody's TypeBool branch and
EncodeBatchColumnar's bool loop) writes bits directly into the output
buffer with no intermediate. The decoder should do the same: read bits
in place and set the target bool value per bit, no []bool in between.

Resolved: readBoolBits is no longer on any decode path. Dense and
Columnar read the packed bool block with readN and unpack each bit
straight into AppendBool — the per-block []bool is gone. (readBoolBits
itself remains for bool_test.go.)

@see #dcd001
@see #dcd002

dcd008.title: Batch decode allocates the return []*DataContainer per call
dcd008.body:
batch.go:DecodeBatchRows does docs := make([]*container.DataContainer,
recordCount) unconditionally — even when the caller will consume and
discard in the same scope. For a 1000-record batch that's 8KB of
pointers per call. Smaller than the per-field issues but constant, and it
sits on the same hot path.

Options: (a) accept it — the slice IS the return value, and callers can't
avoid needing the pointers; (b) pool the slice; (c) offer an iterator API
(DecodeBatchEach(pool, fn)) that avoids the slice entirely for streaming
consumers. (c) is the most useful for large batches — the caller often
wants to process-and-release one record at a time anyway.

@see #dcd005

dcd009.title: Zero-copy string path copies the entire remaining body unconditionally
dcd009.body:
anansi.go:DecodeAnansiInto and batch.go:DecodeBatchRows both do:

    buf := doc.AcquireBacking(body.remaining())
    copy(buf, body.data[body.pos:])

This is correct — the caller's wire buffer must not be retained, so a
snapshot is needed if any string aliases it. But the copy happens even
when the schema has NO string fields, in which case there's nothing to
alias and the copy is pure waste. For a batch of integer-only records the
entire body is copied for no reason.

Precomputed fix: res knows whether any field of the schema is string-typed
(or array-of-string). If not, skip the snapshot. Cheap to check at
resourcesFor time, stored on the slotCodec.

Resolved: slotCodec now carries an `aliasable` bit — true when any field
reachable from the slot (including nested TypeArrayObject element slots)
can produce wire-aliasing strings (TypeString, TypeArrayString, and the
schema-free Record/Unknown carriers). DecodeAnansiInto and DecodeBatchRows
snapshot the caller's wire only when that bit is set; a string-free packet
no longer copies its body at all.

@see #dcd005

dcd010.title: query engine's post-processing path forces []map[string]any, defeating DirectScan
dcd010.body:
engine.go:Query does `d.ToMap()` on every result document before calling
runPostProcessing, and AggregateFunction is typed as
func(records []map[string]any, field string) (any, error). Combined with
InferShape counting aggregations and computed projections as ComputedFields,
this forces the map-shaped path for exactly the workloads where the
container's typed access matters most:

  - sales analytics (SUM/AVG/GROUP BY aggregations)
  - dynamic pricing (computed fields like basePrice * (1 + tax) * discount)

Both are the primary workloads the ERP analytics story depends on.

Fix, in impact order:
  1. Aggregation functions accept []*container.DataContainer (or a columnar
     view) and a DataContainerKey, reading typed slices directly. No map.
  2. Computed field evaluation (FieldReference, FunctionCall, CaseExpression)
     resolves keys to typed container access instead of map[string]any.
  3. Post-processing Filter/Sort use container.Walk instead of ToMap().

InferShape stays accurate afterward — DirectScan() returns false only for
operations that genuinely need map-shaped access (heterogeneous joins).
Aggregations and computed fields remain in the fast path.

Composes with #dcd001–#dcd006: the codec fixes the ends of the pipeline,
this fixes the middle. Both are required for wire-to-result throughput.

dxwlvi.title: Observe Unbounded cache
dxwlvi.body:
In a very complex, dynamic application where module use flactuates at
runtime, a dynamic cache may be more performant memory wise.

g23h8y.title: Inefficient access
g23h8y.body:
Resolved as "already optimal": Tags yields every field/tag pair by
definition, so visiting each one once is O(n) in the size of the output,
which is the best any implementation can do here -- there is no name or
key to look up that could turn this into a sub-linear operation. The
actual per-call overhead #g23h8y was pointing at (repeatedly re-deriving
field/tag structure) is what #5nhvz2 and #0ar5g0 address for the
single-field lookup paths; this function was never doing that redundant
work in the first place, since it already reads directly from the
type's cached structMetadata built once by buildMetadata.

hbivg7.title: Wasted Storage
hbivg7.body:
Resolved: holes is now []DataPoint (type + freed index) instead of
[]DataContainerKey. claimHole reads only .Type() and .ID(), so the
64-bit key's descriptor half was dead weight; DataPoint halves the
per-hole storage. The mechanism is unchanged — if future code wants
same-descriptor hole claiming, the descriptor can return.

hol8mc.title: Implement struct serialization/deserialization
hol8mc.body:
Because schemas can be derived from tagged structs, I would think that
it would be prudent to implement an anansi codec and register it with
codecs. For example

type AnansiCodec interface {
    Marshal(v any) ([]byte, error) // v is a struct with anansi tags
    Unmarshal(data []byte, v any) error // data is a an anansi frame
    Name() string
}
this native loop is not easily discoverable:
pool := document.NewPool(cs, nil)  // check NewPool signature
doc := pool.FromStruct(msg)        // struct → container
wire := doc.ToAnansi(0)            // container → anansi binary

doc2 := pool.FromAnansi(wire)      // anansi binary → container (or pool.New + UnmarshalAnansi)
doc2.BindTo(&msg)                  // container → struct

index-fields-dotted-path.title: index_fields_reference_valid checks top-level names only, rejecting valid dotted index paths

join-projection-ignored.title: Join-level WithProjection is silently ignored
join-projection-ignored.body:
had no explicit projection, the default fallback (this block)
selected ALL columns from ALL schemas, never consulting
JoinConfiguration.Projection.

Fixed: SQLiteSelectProjection now carries q.Joins and the fallback
applies per-join restrictions via joinColumnRestrictions
(include/exclude/alias honored; joins without a projection keep
select-all). Covered by TestSelectJoin_JoinLevelProjection* and
TestJoin_JoinLevelProjection_LimitsColumns.

jq3c65.title: Populate struct
jq3c65.body: Populate this struct and use it properly

metadata-ambiguous-on-joins.title: ensureMetadataProjection injects unqualified _metadata_
metadata-ambiguous-on-joins.body:
include, which SQLite rejects with "ambiguous column name"
when joins put _metadata_ on multiple tables.

Fixed via option (b) at the SQL layer instead of here:
sqliteFactory.resolveInCurrentScope now qualifies any bare
field present on multiple tables with the primary target
(see primaryTarget in sqlite/query/factory.go). This fixes
the injection path and every other bare colliding reference
(filters, sorts) uniformly. Covered by
TestSelectJoin_MetadataDisambiguated and
TestJoin_WithProjection_NoAmbiguousMetadata.

migration-id-sort.title: Migration IDs ordered with localeCompare, not numeric order
migration-id-sort.body:
Migration IDs are Date.now().toString() (set in add()). Two sites used
localeCompare: this method's sort and rollbackToVersion's (now
getRollbackMigrations). localeCompare is locale-aware string
collation, which is correct only while every ID is a same-length
13-digit timestamp. Mixed-length or externally-supplied IDs order
wrongly ("999" > "1000") and collation varies by locale. Fix by
sorting with a numeric comparator (e.g. Number(b.id) - Number(a.id))
when IDs are timestamps, or by issuing sort-safe IDs in add().
Note: schemaVersion sorting/filtering in this file has the same
lexicographic flaw and is being replaced by the core/common/version.go
port (src/version.ts) — that port does not cover migration-ID ordering;
compareMigrationIds handles it here.

physical-name-truncation-collide-496cab4.title: Physical-name truncation collides distinct collections/views onto one table
physical-name-truncation-collide-496cab4.body:
generatePhysicalName caps physical table names at 24 chars, truncating the sanitized logical name to ~18 chars. Distinct collections/views sharing a name prefix + version (e.g. e2e_view_snap-<ts>-<rand>, whose timestamp prefix is stable for days and whose random suffix is truncated off) resolve to the SAME physical table, and CTAS CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS then silently reuses the stale table: reads serve another collection's rows with no error.

Reproduced from hestia E2E: materialized snapshots repeatedly served a 3-row table from an earlier run while their base had 2 rows; green only after a server restart wiped :memory:.

Fix direction: suffix physical names with a uniqueness component (short hash of the full logical name), and/or fail CreateView/DropCollection loudly when the physical table already belongs to another entry instead of reusing it.
Calculate available space for truncation

qpt45v.title: Populate interface
qpt45v.body:
TransactionalEngine defines the set of operations available within a transaction.
It is a limited subset of the full StorageEngine API, ensuring that non-transactional
operations (like creating new collections) cannot be performed within the transaction callback.

sanitize-type-blindness.title: applyPolicy is type-blind and cannot mask non-string fields
sanitize-type-blindness.body:
applyPolicy/hashValue stringify every value (fmt.Sprintf %v), so a policy
match on a non-string slot (array/object/number) produces a string. The
container pipeline (core/document/sanitize.go sanitizeContainerLeaves)
correctly refuses to write a masked string into a non-string slot and
returns "cannot store sanitized value ... in <type> slot", which fails
Sanitize() for the WHOLE document. Real-world fallout: hestia's global
(?i)auth pattern matched the array field `authors` of its dynamic `notes`
collection, so every document failed sanitization and the query API
silently returned data:[] with correct pagination counts (the HTTP layer
drops documents whose Sanitize errors).

Decision (2026-08-22): fix belongs at the app config level for now (keep
masking rules targeted/collection-scoped so patterns only ever hit string
fields); no library change shipped. If this is ever fixed here, likely
shapes are: element-wise masking for arrays of strings, skipping
non-maskable slots with a warning, or schema-type-aware policies threaded
through FieldMaskConfig.

smsm4t.title: FieldDescriptorFromDataPoint is exported and cannot round-trip.
smsm4t.body:
FieldDescriptorFromDataPoint is exported and cannot round-trip.
It rebuilds bits 0–4 as zero — Recursive, Nullable, Terminal, Unique, Deprecated are lost.
If any caller assumes round-trip, they silently get wrong flags.
Three options:
1. Document the lossiness and rename to something like
LossyFieldDescriptorFromDataPoint (or make it package-private).
2. Keep the lossless path (DataContainerKey.Descriptor()) as the only public way
to recover a descriptor, and keep this function internal to the side-table
machinery where the loss is intentional.
3. Evaluate it's actual usage and remove it if possible. The only point of
converting a field descriptor to a datapoint in the first place is to read
metadata in a compiled schema
Right now the function sits between those two worlds without saying which it's in.

xsixg9.title: Error Anti Pattern
xsixg9.body:
There are numerous violation of this principle in this file

@see #1k51l3
